description: We are Team Selene Stargazers-a diverse team passionate about space science, spatial technology , and technical innovation. For the NASA Space Apps Challenge , we developed  'Lunar Indicator'—an automated web platform designed to analyze landing hazards, optimize solar illumination ,and establish critical communication links at the Moon's South Pole . Our team brings together expertise in spatial data research , algorithmic modeling and technical storytelling to make complex ,and space enthusiasts alike. We are looking for a passionate Web Developer who is proficient in Git, GitHub, and website development .
summary:
Lunar Indicator is an offline enabled, web application based navigational tool for the southern pole of the Moon which immediately provides an answer to a key question: where and when is it possible to land?

The user can pick any custom point or one of the 13 Artemis III candidate areas, define a mission period and get hourly information about sunshine, earth view, overlapping of both, slope of terrain and local horizon line along with an unambiguous viability decision and explanation of the decision process. It is possible to compare up to six sites simultaneously allowing quick assessment of tradeoff between solar energy generation capability and visibility from Earth.

Powered by cached JPL Horizons DE441 ephemerides and NASA Moon Trek LOLA topography data it immediately works in any browser without need for installing anything. Since south pole sunshine happens through small time windows and earth is barely visible above the horizon, the right choice of site and landing time will mean the difference between mission success and failure and Lunar Indicator lets mission planners, researchers, and students make that call in seconds.
details:
Lunar Indicator:
Will your lander touch down safely near Shackleton Rim? Was that the landing zone selected yesterday?
Humanity’s gaze turns toward the lunar South Pole, drawn by the promise of water ice and the region’ s profound scientific, logistical, and habitation potential. But between the dream of Artemis bases and the stark reality of the moon’s south pole lies a critical challenge. Because landing there is not only about finding a spot on the map. It is about finding the right moment, when the Sun lights your panels and Earth is still in view. Lunar Indicator is not just a map. It is a testing ground where every proposed south pole site is measured against the unyielding geometry of sun and Earth, then compared against other candidates so you can weigh each trade-off before committing to touchdown.

From Data to Mission Insights :1. A 3D Moon with glowing cap marks 80°S–90°S, and you click any point to send it to dive deep into that point.2. You enter a latitude, longitude and mission dates, or pick a preset site such as Shackleton Rim, Malapert Massif, Faustini or the Apollo sites.3. Hour by hour the app computes Sun and Earth elevation from real JPL Horizons DE441 sub-solar and sub-Earth points, and reads terrain slope plus a 36-direction local horizon from LOLA elevation data through NASA Moon Trek.4. From those it derives sunlight percentage, Earth visibility, their overlap, and compares the average against a 50 percent threshold, with a 15-degree slope cap and a 1.5-degree horizon mask.5. After a result, the page queries JPL Horizons for the real Sun and Earth angles and compares them with the built-in model. It also fetches a LOLA elevation view from NASA Moon Trek.6. You can pick 2–6 sites, including the south-pole sites, the 9 Artemis III candidate regions and the Apollo sites, and set one shared mission window. - It then offers side-by-side or sequential presentation. All of it is pre-cached in a 275 KB data file, so the tool runs offline in any browser with no server and no install.
Significance: Work that normally means cross-checking ephemerides, DEMs and lighting tables for days now takes seconds, and the trade-off between solar power and Earth communication becomes visible instead of buried in numbers. Because the verdict is deterministic and the explanation is generated from the same numbers, anyone can audit it line by line.
Implications: Polar sunlight arrives in short windows and Earth barely clears the horizon, so site and date selection decide whether a lander survives. Lunar Indicator gives mission planners, researchers, students and outreach teams a fast, transparent first look before committing to either.
Tools:HTML5, CSS and vanilla JavaScript; three.js r128 for the 3D Moon; Python 3 standard library for the one-off cache builder; Pillow for icons; Git and GitHub Pages for delivery. No Node.js, no framework, no backend, no database. Data: JPL Horizons, LOLA DEMs, NASA Moon Trek services, the LRO WAC mosaic and the Artemis III region catalog.
Ingenuity: The ephemeris cache is treated as a shipped asset, not a server dependency, so the app is offline-first by design. The verdict is explainable rather than a black box, every result is labelled (cached NASA data, live query or model fallback), and the interface borrows the language of a mission console instead of a dashboard template.
Factors considered:
Unreliable venue Wi-Fi and offline judging, judges verifying numbers against the demo, mobile and small-screen use, data credits and licensing, and the risk of overclaiming, which is why fallbacks are labelled and thresholds are stated openly.
